title: Who will be awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize?
resolution_criteria:
This question will resolve as the recipient of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, expected to be announced by the Norwegian Nobel Committee on October 9, 2026.

If the prize is awarded to an individual not named in the listed options, this question will resolve as **Other individual**. If it is awarded to a non-individual recipient not named in the listed options, it will resolve as **Other organization**.

If no prize is awarded for any reason this question will be **annulled**.
fine_print: If the prize is shared, this question will resolve as the option naming one of the recipients. If more than one recipient is named in the options or if none is, it will resolve according to the recipient listed first in the official announcement by the Norwegian Nobel Committee.

comments.author: sai_39
comments.text:
[PRIO updated its list on 22 September](https://www.prio.org/news/3746), very close to the announcement. Its five themes are coherent:

* Children in war: Mykola Kuleba + Save the Children
* Grassroots humanitarianism: Sudan Emergency Response Rooms
* Press freedom: Committee to Protect Journalists
* International law: ICJ + ICC
* Multilateral cooperation: International Space Station

That does not mean PRIO has inside information. PRIO explicitly says its director has no association with the Nobel Committee and no privileged access. But it is useful because it tries to anticipate what *theme* the Committee might want to emphasize rather than simply compiling famous nominees. The September update itself contains an interesting move: the World Trade Organization was removed and the International Space Station added. The first four themes remained. That makes the repeated presence of Kuleba/Save the Children, ERRs, CPJ and ICJ/ICC noteworthy as an external expert signal, even though it is not a leak.

Overall, the public signals appear to lean toward humanitarian work, protection of civilians, press freedom and international law rather than toward a single high-profile political figure.

My rationales for some of the groups/individuals:

1\) <u>**Doctors without Borders:**</u> [MSF](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/peace/1999/press-release/) won the Peace Prize in 1999. Repeat organisational awards are possible the ICRC but MSF is not on PRIO's updated 2026 list.

2\) <u>**Donald Trump:**</u> Leaders in [Cambodia, Israel and Pakistan](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/some-287-nominated-2026-nobel-peace-prize-trump-likely-among-them-2026-04-30/) publicly said they nominated him. [Reuters' October 1](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/trump-will-not-win-this-years-nobel-peace-prize-he-may-influence-who-does-say-2026-10-01/) reporting says experts it interviewed pointed to the 2026 Iran conflict and the Committee's institutional independence as significant negative considerations.

3\) <u>**ICC/ICJ:**</u> Directly on PRIO's updated shortlist, explicitly as an ICJ + ICC joint possibility. PRIO frames this around international law, dispute resolution and accountability.

4\) <u>**Pope:**</u> Not on the PRIO list, but [Reuters' expert roundup](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/trump-will-not-win-this-years-nobel-peace-prize-he-may-influence-who-does-say-2026-10-01/) identifies Leo as one possible direction. His recent diplomacy has prominently emphasized dialogue, nuclear restraint and ending the Russia-Ukraine war.

5\) <u>**Sudan Emergency Response Rooms:**</u> The ERRs won both the [2025 Rafto Prize](https://www.rafto.no/en/news/the-rafto-prize-2025-to-emergency-response-rooms-of-sudan-err) and [2025 Right Livelihood Award](https://rightlivelihood.org/peace/) for their civilian humanitarian response in Sudan.

6\) <u>**UNRWA:**</u> Its position remains politically contentious, although [AP](https://apnews.com/article/lazzarini-unrwa-hamas-israel-gaza-palestinians-a2fb7495f233cdbe199d571ecfd122f4) reported last week that its infrastructure and personnel remain significant to humanitarian operations.

comments.author: DeRuina
comments.text:
One thing I keep coming back to: PRIO's shortlist has caught the actual laureate only four times in the last twelve years (2014 to 2025), and roughly half of recent winners were barely traded before the announcement (Santos 2016, ICAN 2017, WFP 2020). This year's named options are largely the PRIO and Kalshi favourites, so the two "Other" buckets are effectively a bet on that miss rate continuing. Within those two, I'd split closer to even than the current community does: organisations win about a third of the time overall, and the committee under Frydnes has leaned toward humanitarian and civil-society picks, so an unlisted organisation (CPJ, UNICEF, a Sudan or Gaza relief body) seems at least as likely as an unlisted individual.



There's also a resolution wrinkle worth noting: for a shared prize, the question resolves to whoever the committee names first. A Kuleba plus Save the Children award could land either way depending on the wording. I'd be curious whether anyone has checked how the committee has ordered recent joint awards.

comments.author: Theomachado
comments.text:
# UPDATE:

## Three things have moved since last week.

## First

PRIO's  director published his annual shortlist of who he thinks should win: Mykola Kuleba + Save the Children (Kuleba runs Save Ukraine, which repatriates children deported to Russia), Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms (ERR, the volunteer neighborhood aid networks in Sudan's war), the CPJ (Committee to Protect Journalists), the ICJ + ICC (International Court of Justice and International Criminal Court), and the ISS (International Space Station, as a symbol of US–Russia cooperation).

[![](https://cdn.metaculus.com/user_uploaded/Screenshot_2026-09-29_at_2.18.47AM.png)https://www.prio.org/news/3746](https://www.prio.org/news/3746)

For the purpose of the question this means:

* CPJ, ISS → Other organization
* None → Other individual (Kuleba, ERR, ICC/ICJ and Save the Children are all named options)

## Second

ERR won the Rafto Prize last week; four Rafto laureates have gone on to the Nobel (Suu Kyi, Ramos-Horta, Kim Dae-jung, Ebadi), and it's the Norwegian human-rights prize the committee's milieu actually watches.

## Third

comments.text: Most Peace Prizes go to individuals (7 of the last 10), so I've leaned slightly towards 'Other individual'. Among the named options, Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms look like the strongest candidate.
